channel.title: OWASP Noir
channel.description: Hunt every endpoint in your code. Noir statically analyses source across 32 languages and 263 frameworks, exposing shadow APIs and mapping the attack surface.

item.title: --ai-context and --include-callee: hint and sink for AI code review
item.description: Two v1 flags that ship structured security context to AI source-code analysis instead of raw code.
item.content:encoded:
Since late 2025 or so, AI has changed how a lot of software gets built, and source-code vulnerability analysis has been heading the same way.

A lot of AI-based source-code analysis tools and approaches follow the same shape: feed code in, ask an LLM, get a report back. To actually work well, the LLM needs to know what to look at. Drop the whole codebase on it and you burn tokens while still missing the spots that need attention.

Noir v1 ships two flags that extract that "what to look at" upfront and pack it into the output.

  • --include callee: adds a 1-hop callee graph to each endpoint as a callees array
  • --ai-context: includes the same callee data and sorts it into five security categories under ai_context

--include-callee: who calls whom

The simpler of the two. Parses each endpoint handler body with tree-sitter and pulls out 1-hop callees as {name, path, line}.

$ noir -b ./flask_app --include callee -f json

{
  "url": "/sign",
  "method": "POST",
  "callees": [
    { "name": "get_hash",          "path": "app/utils.py", "line": 3 },
    { "name": "User.query.filter", "path": "app/app.py",   "line": 21 },
    { "name": "User",              "path": "app/app.py",   "line": 24 },
    { "name": "db_session.add",    "path": "app/app.py",   "line": 25 },
    { "name": "db_session.commit", "path": "app/app.py",   "line": 26 }
  ]
}

To an LLM this reads as "to review this endpoint, also look at utils.py:3 and app.py:21,24,25,26". Token-efficient too: instead of shipping the entire codebase, you only need the handler plus those few referenced lines.

--ai-context: same data, sorted into security categories

--ai-context takes the same callee information and runs further analysis to bucket it into five categories.

  • guards: auth middleware / decorators / access-control checks
  • callees: same as above but enriched with a code snippet and a confidence score
  • sinks: potential SQL / command-exec / file-I/O / redirect / template-render endpoints
  • validators: input-validation calls
  • signals: heuristic flags like state_change, credential_input, guard_absence

Running the same Flask /sign POST endpoint with --ai-context

$ noir -b ./flask_app --ai-context -f json

{
  "url": "/sign",
  "method": "POST",
  "ai_context": {
    "sinks": [
      {
        "kind": "sql",
        "name": "query",
        "description": "Potential SQL/data-store sink inferred from code or callee name",
        "path": "app/app.py", "line": 21, "confidence": 78,
        "snippet": "20: password = get_hash(request.form['password'], ...) | 21: if User.query.filter(...).first(): | 22: return render_template('error.html')"
      }
    ],
    "signals": [
      { "kind": "state_change",     "name": "POST",          "confidence": 88 },
      { "kind": "credential_input", "name": "form.password", "confidence": 86 },
      { "kind": "guard_absence",    "name": "POST",          "confidence": 28,
        "description": "No auth guard was detected for this state-changing endpoint." }
    ]
  }
}

What the LLM gets from this single endpoint

  1. There's a credential_input: a password arrives via form
  2. It's a state_change: POST
  3. There's a guard_absence: no auth decorator detected
  4. There's a sql sink: User.query.filter

For a human reviewer and an LLM alike, four signals stacked on one handler send a clear message: review this first. A credential-handling endpoint with no auth on top is priority one; there isn't much to debate.

For contrast, here's a case where --ai-context did pick up auth (flask_auth fixture)

{
  "url": "/profile",
  "method": "GET",
  "ai_context": {
    "guards": [{
      "kind": "auth_guard",
      "name": "flask-login login_required",
      "description": "Protected by flask-login login_required",
      "confidence": 86,
      "snippet": "12: | 13: @login_required | 14: @app.route('/profile') | 15: def profile():"
    }]
  }
}

The @login_required decorator landed in guards. To an LLM that's a negative signal: "this endpoint already has an auth check, focus on other vuln classes instead".

Hint and sink at the same time

The interesting bit is that these flags work as both hint and sink at once.

  • As a hint: pre-curated per-endpoint context narrows the LLM's attention. Instead of "review the entire codebase", it's "this handler plus these files".
  • As a sink (the source-to-sink kind): the sinks bucket lists framework-aware candidates for where data might land. A generic LLM can reason that User.query.filter is SQL, but it burns tokens doing so every time. Noir pre-labels them so the LLM can skip that reasoning step.

The framework-aware part is the big one. The same callee name query means different things in different contexts.

  • Flask + SQLAlchemy: User.query.filter → SQL sink
  • Express + MongoDB: User.find → NoSQL sink
  • A plain LLM either misses the distinction or re-derives it on every pass

Noir identifies the framework in the detector phase, and the augmentor applies that framework's idioms when matching sink / guard patterns. The LLM consumes pre-labeled, framework-aware context instead of raw code.

Recommended use

For an AI-driven code review pipeline

# Every category
noir -b ./app --ai-context -f json

# Narrow to the categories you actually want (saves tokens)
noir -b ./app --ai-context=guards,sinks,signals -f json

# Just callees (lightweight hint)
noir -b ./app --include callee -f json

The full category set is best for the first audit pass. For incremental review or PR-level checks, guards,sinks,signals is usually enough.

What's next

--ai-context's sink and guard patterns are currently regex-based heuristics. We don't do real data-flow tracing; we mark "this looks like a sink" based on callee names and code patterns, and stop there. That's a deliberate trade-off. Precise taint analysis has dedicated tooling, and Noir aims to be the layer that gives that tool (or an LLM) a fast focus point to start from.

From here, the plan is to make the pattern catalogue more framework-aware and add new signal kinds. Feedback and new pattern proposals are always welcome.

item.title: alibi: the endpoints that can't account for themselves
item.description: A companion tool that runs Noir once per view and cross-examines code, docs, traffic, gateway, and infra against each other.
item.content:encoded:
alibi is out: a companion tool that runs Noir once per view of your attack surface and cross-examines the results. It lives at owasp-noir/alibi.

The idea is simple. Noir can already read the same attack surface from five directions:

View Read from
code 200+ analyzers across 33 languages
doc OpenAPI, RAML, WSDL, GraphQL SDL, AsyncAPI, gRPC, Smithy, TypeSpec, OData, OpenRPC
traffic HAR, mitmproxy, Burp, Caido, ZAP, Postman, Insomnia, Bruno, .http
gateway nginx, Apache, Envoy, Kong, Traefik, APISIX, Caddy, Istio, Kubernetes Ingress and Gateway API
infra Terraform, CloudFormation, CDK, Serverless, Vercel, Netlify, Wrangler, Azure Functions, Kamal

Each view is a claim about what exists. The code says "this route is implemented." A contract says "this endpoint is promised." A capture file says "this URL took a real request." An endpoint that shows up in one view should be able to account for itself in the others, and when it can't, someone should go look: that gap is a shadow API, a phantom contract, a gateway rule that routes to nothing. Noir collects all five claims and stops there, by design. alibi asks whether they agree.

The one-scan plan, and why it failed

My first plan was a single scan. Noir labels every endpoint with the technology that found it, so I figured the five views would fall out of one JSON for free.

They don't. Noir deduplicates by (method, url) across every analyzer, and for a discovery tool that's correct: a Flask route and an OpenAPI path spelled identically are one endpoint. For a comparison it's a problem, and it gets worse exactly when things are going well: the better two views agree, the more of their endpoints merge into single records, and the corroboration you wanted to measure disappears. Scan casdoor whole and you get 372 code endpoints against 9 documented ones. Scan its swagger/ directory alone and the spec holds 235.

So alibi runs Noir once per view, restricting each pass with --only-techs, and joins the results itself. Noir needed no changes for any of this, and alibi parses no API formats of its own. Its only input is Noir's JSON.

That's also the reason it's a separate repository, and a Python one. Noir grew from 19k to 198k lines in about a year. I'd rather grow the ecosystem sideways than keep growing the binary, and the contribution bar for a comparison tool should be low.

What a run looks like

$ alibi scan ./casdoor
alibi  ·  1 source  ·  377 endpoints

  code 372   doc 235

  230 corroborated -- vouched for by more than one view

  19 endpoints nearly matched another view -- these may be matching failures, not real gaps

SHADOW  Shadow API -- Implemented, but no contract describes it
  134 findings  ·  4 critical, 57 high, 62 medium, 11 low

  critical POST    /api/upload-groups        router.go:87
           upload paths carry more consequence than reads
  critical POST    /api/upload-permissions   router.go:208

Eight rules ship: SHADOW, PHANTOM, ORPHAN, LIVE_UNDOC, DANGLING, DRIFT, UNEXPOSED, COLD. Severity then shifts on what Noir's taggers saw on the endpoint: file uploads, personal data, state-changing methods, signs of authentication.

Most of the work wasn't the comparison

Joining five endpoint lists is a weekend project. The real work was keeping the report honest, and every guard in alibi exists because a real repository produced a confident wrong answer first.

The first full run on casdoor marked nearly half the findings critical. The promotion rule was "no sign of authentication", and Noir's auth taggers had tagged nine endpoints out of almost four hundred, so "no sign" was true nearly everywhere and meant nothing. The rule now runs the other way: the presence of a signal moves severity, and an adjustment keyed to a missing tag applies only when that tag exists somewhere in the scan.

Argo CD reported 58 shadow APIs and 198 phantom contracts, none of them real. Its Go code registers /api; its OpenAPI documents 198 paths beneath it. Same surface, two granularities, not a single shared endpoint. Zero overlap between two populated views now reads as "this comparison failed", so the rules hold back and the report explains why instead of flooding.

NetBox nearly shipped the worst answer of all. Its API documentation is one 12.35MB OpenAPI file, Noir skipped it for exceeding the file-size cap, and the draft report concluded that the project documents nothing. That's not an incomplete answer, it's a wrong one, delivered with full confidence. Noir now gives specification documents their own size budget (#2671), and alibi prints whatever Noir reported it couldn't read above the findings, because a missing view and an empty view mean opposite things.

The same caution runs through the rest. A finding whose endpoint nearly matches another view (same path under a different verb, a parameter where the other side has a literal) is demoted and flagged, because "in code but not in the docs" is indistinguishable from "in both, but alibi failed to line them up". Snapshots record which rules actually evaluated, because dropping the contracts directory from one run makes SHADOW evaluate nothing, and to a naive diff that looks exactly like every shadow API having been closed.

Under all of it sits one normalization rule: a path parameter's name is not part of its identity. /users/<int:user_id>, /users/{id} and /users/:id describe the same slot; what matters is its position and whether it spans a /. Before trusting that rule I ran it over every route fixture in Noir's own test tree, 3,195 URLs across 33 languages.

Where it stops

alibi compares what Noir can read, and a view read at the wrong granularity is worse than one not read at all. Argo CD sits at that ceiling above. authentik assembles its URLconf at runtime by importing every installed app's urls module, which no static reader can follow. flipt mounts a gRPC gateway, so its Go source holds exactly one route. All three are held back by the overlap guard, and the report names the reason rather than inventing findings.

NetBox is the case that shows the intended workflow, though. One repository, two surfaces: a server-rendered web UI and a DRF REST API, and only the second has a contract. Scanned whole it reports 746 findings, most of them the true but useless observation that a web UI is not in an API specification. Scoped to what the contract covers:

$ alibi scan ./netbox --ignore '^/(?!api/)'

Three shadow APIs remain (/api/plugins, /api/schema/redoc, /api/schema/swagger-ui), all genuinely served and all genuinely absent from the schema.

Building this fed fixes back into Noir along the way: split OpenAPI documents that $ref their operations out to other files (#2673), the DRF surface a Django project actually exposes (#2672), and the spec size budget above. That loop, a companion tool stress-testing the scanner, may turn out to be alibi's second job.

Try it

uv tool install noir-alibi   # or: pipx install noir-alibi
alibi scan ./service ./contracts ./prod.har

It needs noir 1.0.0 or newer on PATH. -f sarif uploads to code scanning, --fail-on high gates a build, and an .alibi.yml next to the source suppresses the gaps that are intentional.

It's early. If alibi tells you something that isn't true, that's exactly the kind of bug the whole tool is organized around catching, so please open an issue. Happy hunting :D

item.title: Noir v1.0: Major bump, compat-first
item.description: Why 1.x now, and how the v0 surface stayed intact.
item.content:encoded:
Noir v1.0 is out.

It's been roughly four years since the first commit landed in my personal repo, and now we're cutting it as an official release.

I could have kept extending the 0.x line, but there were two reasons to bump the major.

  1. Stability: around v0.30 it reached the point where adding a new framework no longer breaks existing analysis results. Analyzer contracts, output schema, on-disk paths: the core interfaces have settled, and it felt like the right time to call it 1.x.
  2. Sub-commands: v0's CLI was flag-only. With more ancillary features coming (cache, rules, config), flags alone were hitting their limits. v1 introduces a verb-based structure: noir scan / list / cache / config / rules / completion / version / help.

Outside those two decisions, almost every change was designed around v0 compatibility. v0 call shapes like noir -b ./app -P -f json route automatically into the scan subcommand, and renamed flags keep their old names as silent aliases. The only thing that breaks explicitly is --ollama / --ollama-model, both deprecated since 2024.

Most v0 scripts run on v1 without modification. That's the whole point of this release.

The full change list and the few items that need migration are collected in the CHANGELOG v1.0.0.

Upgrades use the same paths as always:

brew upgrade noir
# or
docker pull ghcr.io/owasp-noir/noir:1.0.0
# or
gh release download v1.0.0 -R owasp-noir/noir

Spot a bug or have feedback? File it on GitHub Issues. Happy hunting :D

item.title: Fill the blanks once: --pvalue across curl, collections, and probes
item.description: One set of parameter placeholders that flows into curl, Postman, OpenAPI, status-code probes, and Burp/ZAP replay.
item.content:encoded:
If you've ever run noir scan ./app -f curl, you know the result: a long list of /users/{id}?limit= lines. Great as a map of the app, but you can't paste a single one of them into a terminal and expect a real response.

-f postman gives you the same blanks in a different wrapper. --probe either sends the literal {id} and collects 404s, or, for GET/HEAD/OPTIONS only, quietly fills in 1 or noir. Three consumers, each with its own idea of what a parameter should hold.

--pvalue settles that in one place. You declare the values once, and the optimizer writes them into every parameter before any formatter or deliverer gets to see the endpoint list. Same scan, same values, no matter where the output ends up.

The flag

It's repeatable. Each occurrence is TYPE=VALUE, or just VALUE if you want it applied to every type:

noir scan ./app -f curl -u https://api.example.com \
  --pvalue "path=id=42" \
  --pvalue "query=limit=10" \
  --pvalue "header=Authorization=Bearer replace-me"
TYPE Scope
any (or omit the type) Every parameter type
query / form / json / header / cookie / path That bucket only

VALUE itself comes in two shapes:

Form Behavior
42 Every parameter of the targeted type
id=42 or id:42 Only parameters named id

The substitution happens while the endpoint list is being cleaned up, so it lands ahead of curl, HTTPie, PowerShell, OpenAPI, Postman, JSON and YAML output, and ahead of probing and export too. For the format side see cURL / HTTPie / PowerShell; for probing see Delivering Results.

How rules are picked

Type-specific rules win over the global any list, so --pvalue path=… beats a bare --pvalue test for path parameters. Within a type, a rule that names the parameter wins over a catch-all, and the order you pass the flags in doesn't matter:

# limit → 10; everything else in query → 1
noir scan ./app -f curl -u https://api.example.com \
  --pvalue "query=1" \
  --pvalue "query=limit=10"

Swap those two lines and you get the same result. If you declare two rules for the same name, the first one wins, but that's a case you rarely want anyway.

Where the same declaration pays off

Curl you can actually paste

noir scan ./api -f curl -u https://staging.example.com \
  --pvalue "path=id=42" \
  --pvalue "path=slug=demo" \
  --pvalue "query=1" \
  --pvalue "header=Authorization=Bearer $STAGING_TOKEN" \
  -o /tmp/api.curl.sh

source it and go. Path templates are already substituted in the URLs the curl builder emits, so there's no sed pass over {id} afterwards.

Postman / OpenAPI for the rest of the team

noir scan ./api -f postman -u https://staging.example.com \
  --pvalue "path=id=42" \
  --pvalue "query=limit=10" \
  --pvalue "header=Authorization=Bearer replace-me" \
  -o /tmp/api.postman.json

noir scan ./api -f oas3 -u https://staging.example.com \
  --pvalue "path=id=42" \
  --pvalue "query=limit=10" \
  -o /tmp/api.openapi.json

Same --pvalue block as the curl run. Reviewers import one collection, CI diffs the OpenAPI against yesterday's, and the placeholders stay identical across formats.

Live status codes, and optionally a proxy

# Attach observed status codes; drop the obvious misses
noir scan ./api -u https://staging.example.com \
  --status-codes --exclude-codes 404,502 \
  --pvalue "path=id=42" \
  --pvalue "query=1" \
  -f json -o /tmp/live.json

# Send only reads through Burp/ZAP so the target isn't hit twice as hard
noir scan ./api -u https://staging.example.com \
  --probe-via http://127.0.0.1:8080 \
  --probe-match "GET" \
  --pvalue "path=id=42" \
  --pvalue "header=Authorization=Bearer $STAGING_TOKEN"

--status-codes, --probe and --probe-via all need -u.

One thing worth knowing before you probe: without --pvalue path=…, Noir only auto-fills path parameters on read-only verbs (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS), using 1 or noir. POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE keep the literal template, so a probe can't turn into DELETE /users/1 by accident. An explicit --pvalue path=id=42 removes that guard and applies to every verb, writes included. If that's what you want, fine. If not, keep writes out with --probe-skip "POST" or --probe-skip "DELETE" until you're ready.

Put the defaults in a config file

The same keys live in the config file, which saves repeating the flags on every CI job:

url: "https://staging.example.com"
format: "json"
status_codes: true
exclude_codes: "404,502"
set_pvalue_path:
  - "id=42"
  - "slug=demo"
set_pvalue_query:
  - "limit=10"
  - "1"
set_pvalue_header:
  - "X-Debug-Tenant=noir-ci"

noir config init
noir scan ./api --config-file ./ci/noir.yaml

A --pvalue on the command line still wins when a one-off run needs a different id. See Configuration file and noir config.

Things that trip people up

  • Nameless parameters get nothing. If an analyzer knows a parameter exists but not what it's called, it's dropped before --pvalue runs. You won't see a stray =42 in the curl output.
  • body lands in json. Parameters recorded as body are normalized into the buckets the optimizer knows, so --pvalue json=… reaches them. For new scripts, use --pvalue TYPE=VAL rather than the old --set-pvalue-* aliases.
  • Headers follow -u. --probe-header and --pvalue header=… on probe payloads are aimed at the -u host. Endpoints that already carry an absolute host from the source keep that host and don't get those headers. Export destinations you named yourself still do.
  • Secrets don't belong in committed YAML. Expand them in CI (--pvalue "header=Authorization=Bearer $TOKEN") instead of baking tokens into ci/noir.yaml.

Wrapping up

Discovery output without values is a map with no street numbers. --pvalue lets you number them once and reuse the result across curl, collections, OpenAPI, status-code filtering and proxy replay. Be deliberate about write verbs when probing, and once the team agrees on the placeholders, move them into the config file.

item.title: After the endpoint list: query, reach, and trace
item.description: Use Noir's endpoint report to narrow a review, find routes connected to a source file, and match a request to its route.
item.content:encoded:
An endpoint list is a good place to start a review. Then you find a shared helper, a suspicious request, or a group of routes that needs a closer look. Reading the whole list again does not answer those questions.

Noir's query, reach, and trace let you start with what you already know. A filter, a source file, or a concrete request can lead you to the next piece of code to read.

Keep the report, change the question

Each command can scan a codebase directly. During a review, though, the questions keep changing. Saving a report lets you ask them without scanning again.

The examples below use the Flask callee fixture in the Noir repository. They were run with Noir 1.5.0, from the repository root, with noir on PATH. This fixture has a form handler, an order lookup, and helpers that both handlers call. No running Flask application is needed.

cd spec/functional_test/fixtures/python/flask_callees
noir scan . --ai-context --include callee -f json \
	-o /tmp/noir-review.json --no-log > /dev/null

--ai-context collects static review context. It does not need an AI provider. --include callee keeps the recorded calls in the report too. The stdout redirect hides the duplicate report that scan prints while -o saves it.

There is a difference between a live scan and --from. A live query command enables all AI context and callee collection implicitly. A saved report contains only what the original scan collected. Reading it does not add missing guards or sinks, and changing the application does not update the report. Regenerate it when the source changes.

Query gives the review a starting point

Suppose you want to inspect POST handlers that accept a form field named name, without a recorded authentication or authorization guard.

noir query --method POST --no-guard --param name --param-type form \
	--from /tmp/noir-review.json -f text

POST /users  ./app.py:7  python_flask  handler=create_user@./app.py:8  signals=guard_absence

That leaves create_user at app.py:8 to read. Different filters combine with AND. Values within a comma-separated filter combine with OR, so --method GET,POST accepts either method. When you specify both a parameter name and type, the same parameter must satisfy both.

--no-guard means Noir recorded no authentication or authorization guard. It does not prove that the route is public. Unresolved middleware or an upstream gateway can change the answer. Rate limiting and CSRF checks do not count as authentication guards either.

If your report has database sinks, --sink sql can narrow the review further. A recorded sink is a reason to read the code, not a finding of SQL injection.

Reach starts where the code changed

Now suppose the change is in run_sql_query, defined at helpers.py:5. Which endpoints need another look?

noir reach helpers.py:5 --from /tmp/noir-review.json -f text

POST /users  ./app.py:7  python_flask  handler=create_user@./app.py:8  signals=guard_absence  via=callee:run_sql_query@./helpers.py:5,callee:build_user_query@./helpers.py:1,callee:notify_admin@./helpers.py:10,callee:log_audit@./helpers.py:14
GET /orders/<order_id>  ./app.py:17  python_flask  handler=get_order@./app.py:18  signals=path_param,idor  via=callee:run_sql_query@./helpers.py:5,callee:build_user_query@./helpers.py:1

Both /users and /orders/<order_id> appear. Their via fields point to recorded callees in helpers.py, with run_sql_query first because its definition is closest to the requested line.

The line number ranks matches. It does not restrict the result to a function containing that line. Noir records declaration locations rather than complete function spans. JSON and JSONL output also include nearest_line when you supply a line number.

reach uses path suffixes, so helpers.py is enough here. In a larger repository, use a longer suffix to distinguish files with the same name. It checks recorded route, handler, callee, guard, source, sink, and validator locations. It is not a complete call graph, and it does not follow inheritance or dynamic loading. An empty result means no recorded connection matched, not that a change cannot affect a route.

Trace starts with the request you have

A proxy log usually has a concrete path, while the application declares a route template. Here is the order lookup from the same report:

noir trace "GET /orders/42" --from /tmp/noir-review.json -f text

GET /orders/<order_id>  ./app.py:17  python_flask  matched_by=pattern  handler=get_order@./app.py:18  signals=path_param,idor

matched_by=pattern explains why /orders/42 matches /orders/<order_id>. This is a lookup in the saved report. It sends no HTTP request.

Include the method when you know it. Without a method, Noir returns matching routes across methods. HEAD can match a GET route. If several routes match, the most specific matches come first.

A catch-all can accept a misspelled path too. When only wildcard or prefix routes match, trace also looks for nearby candidates. A complete miss exits with code 1 and includes any candidates it found. JSON and JSONL output carry the full matched endpoint under endpoint, so you can inspect its recorded parameters and context without another scan.

Use the result to choose what to read next

There is no required order. Start with query when you know a property, reach when you have a changed file, or trace when you have a request. Then check the evidence against the code.

Text output keeps the terminal readable. JSONL is the default for scripts, and --full adds the full endpoint record to query and reach results. --limit caps the printed rows. --count prints a count, but if you combine the two, it counts only the limited rows. All three commands exit with code 1 when nothing matches.

Keep scan paths and scan-only flags on the original scan. Noir rejects them alongside --from, because that command reads a report rather than scanning a directory. The CLI reference has the full filter list and output options.

item.title: Welcome to the Noir blog
item.description: A new space for release deep dives, performance notes, design rationale, and the writing that doesn't fit in a changelog.
item.content:encoded:
Hi, this is hahwul. I've been writing Noir tips and notes on my personal blog for a while, but it felt better to have an official channel for it, so we're opening a blog space inside the project docs.

It's a small experimental section sitting alongside the documentation, meant to collect the kinds of writing that don't quite fit into release notes or reference pages. Better here than scattered across PR descriptions.

What you'll find here

  • Release deep dives: what landed in recent versions, the background, and the trade-offs we picked.
  • Performance and accuracy investigations: when a benchmark or a false-positive sweep turns up something worth writing about, we'll post it.
  • Framework coverage notes: the parsing edge cases we run into while adding support for a new Rust/Python/JVM framework.
  • Design rationale: why the analyzer pipeline, optimizer passes, and AI context ended up shaped the way they are.
  • Tips: practical know-how for getting more out of Noir in everyday use.

How it fits the rest of the docs

  • The Get Started guide stays the canonical place to learn the tool.
  • The Usage section keeps reference material: flags, supported frameworks, output formats.
  • The blog supplements both with narrative content. If a topic graduates into something every user should know, it migrates into the docs.

Cadence

There's no schedule. Posts go up when there's something to write about. For regular updates, follow the GitHub releases; check back here once in a while for the longer reads.

If you'd like to contribute a post (write about how you use Noir, share a CI integration, or unpack a framework's routing model), open a PR with a draft. Authors get a card next to the post.
